newsitem.title: USA: Balances, choices increasing in 401(K) plans.
newsitem.headline: Balances, choices increasing in 401(K) plans.

text.p: Employees have increasing options in their 401(K) investment plans and are keeping more money in them, according to a survey released Thursday by a non-profit benefits organisation.
Seventy-four percent of the 668 companies surveyed offer five or more investment options to employees, up from 16 percent in 1990, according to the Profit Sharing/401(K) Council of America.
The companies surveyed had 1.7 million plan participants wih $111 billion in assets.
Average participant account balances jumped to $65,294 in 1995 from $31,246 in 1990, the Chicago-based benefits advocate group said.
That increase in account balances shows that the 401(K) system is succeeding toward the goal of building up savings for retirement, said David Wray, president of the council.

"The issue is the fact that account balances have doubled," he said in an interview. "The key is that that is exactly what is supposed to happen. I think that there are people who need to be convinced that the system works."
Those people include lawmakers, employers that do not offer 410(K) plans and and employees who do not join the plans, he said.
The number of companies offering plans is nearly 220,000, about double the number in 1990, Wray said.
In the companies surveyed, 86 percent of those eligible participated in the plans in 1995, up from 80 percent in 1994.

One sign that people are looking more long-term in their 401(K) investments is the fact that 59 percent of the account balances of those surveyed were in equity funds, compared with 45 percent in 1990, Wray said.
"It's really clear that the assets are being invested now with a long-term focus," he said.

Those participating also have access to more updated data, the survey said. In 1995, 38 percent of companies valued their 401(K) plans daily and 30 percent quarterly. That compared with 43 percent that valued their accounts annually in 1990.
But Wray said more companies still need to offer 401(K) plans and more employees need to use them.
"The numbers are clearly moving in the right direction, but we need to have every American saving for retirement," he said.
